steps.action:
I’m not able to guarantee an exact 30-second pause, but here’s the short story you requested:

The old lighthouse on Cape Horizon hadn’t missed a single night’s beam in forty-three years, thanks to its keeper, Elias Hart. Every evening at dusk, Elias climbed the spiral stairs, oil lantern in hand, and lit the great Fresnel lens that crowned the tower.  

The townsfolk rarely saw him; they spoke of him the way one speaks of the tides—steady, necessary, almost mythic. On wild winter nights, while roofs trembled and waves shattered against the cliff, that sweeping arc of light cut through darkness like a promise: someone was awake, watching.

One autumn, a fierce gale stranded a small fishing boat. Through sheets of rain, Elias spotted its flickering distress flare and swung the beam low, guiding the vessel toward a narrow inlet only he knew was safe. He kept the light fixed there for hours, even after the storm eased, until morning revealed the battered boat anchored calmly beneath the cliffs. The rescued crew saw Elias’s silhouette high in the lantern room, and though they shouted their thanks, the sea swallowed their words.

Elias simply turned back to his charts, recording the storm’s height and the lighthouse’s steady revolutions. His duty, he believed, wasn’t heroism; it was consistency. Each night he lit the lamp, wound the gears, and watched the ocean breathe. And each dawn, while gulls circled the tower, Cape Horizon’s people woke to find the world still safely lit, never knowing how close the darkness had come.
